q: You make 1000 dogs with `new Dog("Rex")`. How many copies of the method `bark` exist?
options: Two: one on `Dog` and one on `Object`
None, because `bark` is made only when it is called
why: A class is a function. Its methods sit once on `Dog.prototype`. Each dog keeps only its own data and one hidden link to that object.

q: What does this print? Type the two answers with a space between them.
answer: Rex makes a sound, woof true
why: `rex.speak()` finds Dog's `speak` first. `super.speak()` starts the search one step up, at `Animal.prototype`, and gives `"Rex makes a sound"`. Then Dog adds `", woof"`. `rex instanceof Animal` is `true`, because `Animal.prototype` is on the chain of `rex`.

options: A `ReferenceError`: `this` is locked until `super()` has run
why: In a child class, the parent constructor makes the object. Before `super()` returns, there is no object for `this` to be. Fix: call `super(name)` first.

q: In a child class, you can use `this` in the constructor before you call `super()`.
why: No. The parent constructor makes the object. Until `super()` runs, `this` is locked, and using it throws a `ReferenceError`.

q: Put the steps of `new Dog("Rex")` in the right order. `Dog extends Animal`.
items: `new Dog("Rex")` starts Dog's constructor, with `this` locked
`super(name)` runs Animal's constructor, which makes the empty object
`this.name = name` writes the name on that object, and `this` is unlocked in Dog
`this.tricks = 0` runs, and `new` gives back the object
why: A child class does not make the object. The parent does, and its hidden link points at `Dog.prototype` because `new` was called on `Dog`.

q: Which of these let you call the method later without losing `this`?
options: Write the method as an arrow field: `inc = () => { this.count++; };`
why: The arrow wrapper calls with a dot. `bind` locks `this`. An arrow field keeps `this`, but it makes one function for every instance. `const f = c.inc` leaves the object behind.

q: A property named `_balance` is really private. Outside code cannot read it.
why: No. `_balance` is only a polite sign. It is a normal property, and outside code can read and change it. Only a `#balance` slot is really private.

options: A `SyntaxError`: a `#` name belongs only to the class body where it is written
why: The file does not even start. A `#` name is not on the prototype chain. Fix: the parent offers a getter, `get balance() { return this.#balance; }`, and the child reads `this.balance`.

q: Which of these are true about a `class`?
options: Its methods sit once on the prototype, not on each instance
You must call it with `new`. Without `new` it throws a `TypeError`
Class code is not strict, so `this` becomes the global object in a plain call
why: A class is a shorter way to write a constructor function and its prototype, plus safety rules: `new` is required, and the code is always strict. So a lost `this` is `undefined`, not the global object.
